title: The end of cheap peace in East Asia
gist: Markets price the Western Pacific as a binary — peace or war — and therefore miss the compounding cost of the in-between: redundancy capex at TSMC, rare-earth risk language spreading through Tokyo filings, latent Taiwan Strait insurance repricing, and the fastest Asian defence spending rise since 2009. The old bargain in which efficiency purchased stability has expired; firms now fund efficiency and security separately, and are staying in East Asia while paying more.

insights.claim: Chinese and Japanese coastguard vessels squared off near the Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands in July 2026 with each side claiming to have driven the other away, and the story left the headlines within a day.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Habituation to maritime standoffs suppresses the risk premium markets attach to them even as the underlying frequency rises.
insights.quote: Standoffs like this have become routine. But that routine is precisely the problem.
insights.locator: Earlier this month, Chinese and Japanese coastguard vessels

insights.claim: Markets price East Asia too narrowly as either continued peace or erupting war, missing the intermediate state in which companies, governments and investors pay more to keep an indispensable but less secure system running.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: The tradeable insight is not war probability but the accumulating margin and capex drag of grey-zone risk — a slow, persistent hit to Asian industrial returns.
insights.quote: The Western Pacific is still at peace – but the peace is no longer cheap.
insights.locator: Standoffs like this have become routine

insights.claim: The decades-old assumption that efficiency itself produces stability — deeper trade links raising the cost of conflict — is expiring, because the same networks that carried efficiency gains now carry political shocks.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Interdependence has flipped from a stabiliser to a transmission channel — reprice supply-chain depth as a vulnerability rather than a moat.
insights.quote: Export controls, licensing rules, investment screening, and coastguard enforcement have turned supply chains into transmission belts for state pressure.
insights.locator: For decades, multinationals concentrated advanced manufacturing

insights.claim: The new bargain in East Asia is that efficiency still brings profits but security must be paid for separately, replacing the old bargain in which efficiency brought stability.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A permanent new cost line for Asia-exposed manufacturers — model security spend as structural opex/capex, not a cyclical one-off.
insights.quote: The old bargain was simple: efficiency brought stability. The new bargain is harsher: efficiency still brings profits, but security must be paid for separately.
insights.locator: Trade still constrains conflict

insights.claim: Markets are good at pricing visible earnings and liquidity flows but poor at pricing the slow accumulation of redundancy costs.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Names carrying heavy duplication capex may look cheap on forward earnings while structurally impairing returns on capital — screen for redundancy spend, not just growth.
insights.quote: Markets are good at pricing visible earnings and liquidity flows. They are less good at pricing the slow accumulation of redundancy costs.
insights.locator: The market signal is therefore mixed, not absent

insights.claim: Taiwan, specifically TSMC, accounts for more than 90% of the world's most advanced chipmaking capacity — a concentration that made sense under an efficiency priority but reads as single-point vulnerability under a security priority.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: The single largest concentration risk in global manufacturing; any Taiwan Strait disruption is a systemic, not sectoral, event.
insights.quote: That concentration made sense when the priority was efficiency. It looks very different when the priority is reducing single-point vulnerability.
insights.locator: Semiconductors show the shift most clearly

insights.claim: TSMC's expansion in the United States plus fabs in Japan and Germany replicates capacity that was once concentrated in a single hyper-efficient ecosystem, which is inherently expensive duplication rather than growth.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Geographic diversification of leading-edge fabs is dilutive to blended margins — expect structurally lower semiconductor sector returns on invested capital.
insights.locator: TSMC’s expansion in the United States

insights.claim: TSMC CEO C.C. Wei has said each construction step in Arizona takes at least twice as long as in Taiwan, citing permitting, labour shortages and supply gaps.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A hard 2x execution-time penalty on US reshoring — the practical ceiling on how fast Western fab capacity can actually come online, subsidies notwithstanding.
insights.quote: Chief executive C.C. Wei has said each construction step in Arizona takes at least twice as long as in Taiwan
insights.locator: Redundancy is expensive

insights.claim: Billions in subsidies have supported TSMC's Arizona investment but subsidies do not erase the cost of rebuilding an entire supplier ecosystem, so security is purchased at the price of efficiency.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Public subsidy headlines overstate the de-risking achieved; the ecosystem gap, not the capital gap, is the binding constraint on reshoring.
insights.quote: Security can be bought – at the cost of efficiency.
insights.locator: TSMC’s Arizona investment has benefited from billions in subsidies

insights.claim: Apple's shift of iPhone production for the US market to India is a response to tariffs and concentration risk in China rather than a search for cheaper labour.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Relocation decisions are now driven by policy risk, not unit cost — expect further moves that raise landed cost and compress hardware gross margins.
insights.quote: not a search for cheaper labour but a response to tariffs and concentration risk in China
insights.locator: Apple’s shift of iPhone production

themes.theme: Rare earths and the disclosure signal in Japan

insights.claim: Since Beijing tightened rare earth export controls on Japan in January 2026, mentions of rare-earth risk in Tokyo Stock Exchange filings have doubled.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Corporate disclosure language is a measurable leading indicator of coercion exposure — a screenable dataset before earnings impacts appear.
insights.quote: mentions of rare-earth risk in Tokyo Stock Exchange filings have doubled
insights.locator: Japan is seeing the same bill through critical minerals

insights.claim: Two-thirds of some 200 recent Tokyo Stock Exchange filings said Chinese rare-earth curbs are already hurting business or pose a credible risk, even though few report a major earnings hit yet.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A wide gap between acknowledged risk and realised P&L damage — the earnings impact is pending, not absent, for Japanese industrials.
insights.quote: two-thirds of some 200 recent filings said the curbs are already hurting business or pose a credible risk
insights.locator: Since Beijing tightened rare earth export controls

insights.claim: Japanese firms are absorbing rare-earth coercion through altered production plans, alternative sourcing and more careful inventory management — the cost of operating under persistent coercive risk rather than the cost of war.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Higher working capital and buffer inventory become permanent features of Japanese industrial balance sheets — a drag on cash conversion.
insights.quote: This is not the cost of war but rather the cost of operating under persistent coercive risk.
insights.locator: But the risk has entered financial language

themes.theme: Flows versus fundamentals in Asian equities

insights.claim: Taiwan's equity market rose more than 60% in the first half of 2026 on artificial intelligence demand, even as foreign investors pulled a record US$137 billion from emerging Asian equities.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: AI demand is overwhelming geopolitical outflows in Taiwanese pricing — a fragile equilibrium if the AI capex cycle cools while the risk remains.
insights.quote: Taiwan’s equity market rose more than 60% in the first half of this year on demand for artificial intelligence
insights.locator: The market signal is therefore mixed, not absent

insights.claim: Taiwan and South Korea bore the brunt of the record foreign outflow from emerging Asian equities as investors trimmed crowded chip positions.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Positioning in Asian chip names has been crowded and is being reduced — a flow headwind independent of earnings momentum.
insights.quote: with Taiwan and South Korea bearing the brunt as investors trimmed crowded chip positions
insights.locator: even as foreign investors pulled a record US$137 billion

themes.theme: Taiwan Strait shipping and the insurance tripwire

insights.claim: Some US$2.4 trillion in goods — more than a fifth of global maritime trade — moved through the Taiwan Strait in 2024, a figure that reads as efficiency while the route stays open and as exposure if grey-zone pressure alters shipping expectations.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Sizes the systemic trade exposure to a single chokepoint; any sustained disruption is a global inflation and logistics event, not a regional one.
insights.quote: As long as the route stays open, that figure looks like proof of efficiency. If grey-zone pressure begins to affect shipping expectations, it becomes an exposure.
insights.locator: Shipping and insurance make the problem concrete

insights.claim: In the Red Sea, war-risk premiums ran at a nominal 0.05% of hull value before the Houthi attacks and by early 2024 underwriters were quoting as much as 1% for a single seven-day passage — a twentyfold jump within months.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete magnitude and speed for insurance repricing under maritime threat — the template for modelling a Taiwan Strait shock.
insights.quote: by early 2024, underwriters were quoting as much as 1% for a single seven-day passage – a twentyfold jump in months
insights.locator: The Red Sea offered a preview

insights.claim: No insurer reprices the Taiwan Strait after every standoff, but none can leave the scenario out of its stress tests, and the Red Sea showed that once underwriting conditions trip the adjustment takes weeks rather than decades.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Taiwan Strait risk is a step-function, not a gradual repricing — hedges must be in place before the trigger because the adjustment window is days-to-weeks.
insights.quote: the Red Sea showed that once underwriting conditions trip, adjustment takes weeks, not decades
insights.locator: No insurer reprices the Taiwan Strait after every standoff

insights.claim: Global military spending reached US$2.887 trillion in 2025, with Asia and Oceania recording the fastest annual rise since 2009.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Confirms Asia-Pacific as the fastest-growing defence market — a multi-year structural tailwind for regional defence suppliers.
insights.quote: Global military spending reached US$2.887 trillion in 2025
insights.locator: Governments are paying too

insights.claim: Japan has pledged to hit its defence target of 2% of GDP two years early and Taiwan's defence budget grew 14% last year.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Concrete acceleration in the two frontline budgets — fiscal room for other priorities narrows in both, with implications for JGB supply and Taiwanese fiscal policy.
insights.quote: Taiwan’s defence budget grew 14% last year.
insights.locator: Japan has pledged to hit its defence target

insights.claim: Policymakers in East Asia no longer treat economic interdependence as a sufficient substitute for security, and are buying security back through defence budgets, subsidies and stockpiles.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: The intellectual foundation of the post-1990s Asian trade order has been abandoned by its own policymakers — a durable regime change for regional fiscal and industrial policy.
insights.quote: Policymakers no longer treat interdependence as a sufficient substitute for security.
insights.locator: Policymakers no longer treat interdependence

insights.claim: Capital is not leaving East Asia because the engineers, supplier networks and end markets remain irreplaceable — which is precisely why companies are staying and paying more.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Do not trade the decoupling narrative as an exodus; the correct expression is margin compression and higher capex in place, not divestment.
insights.quote: The choice was never efficiency or security. Firms now fund both at once.
insights.locator: None of this means capital is leaving East Asia
